newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says govt not Bank of Italy decides budget.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says govt not Bank of Italy decides budget.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Friday his government would decide on its own how much to slice from the 1997 budget deficit and was not obliged to listen to the Bank of Italy regarding the size of a mini-budget.
"The Bank of Italy can say whatever it wants, but I'm the one who makes the budget," Prodi told state television RAI in an interview to be broadcast later in the day.

In its semi-annual report issued on Friday, the Bank of Italy said 15 trillion lire must be sliced from the budget deficit if Italy were to cut its deficit to GDP ratio to the three percent required by the Maastricht Treaty on European economic and monetary union.
Prodi said the ratio was currently about 3.3 to 3.4 percent and that the mini-budget would bring it down to three percent. But he insisted that the final figure of the package was still not decided.
"Just because the Bank of Italy gives this figure (15 trillion lire) doesn't mean we're obliged (to meet it)," Prodi said.
"Within a few weeks we will have the exact figure and I have said that, for now, we are looking at a figure that ranges between six trillion and 14.5 trillion lire," he said.
Prodi later qualified his remarks, saying that he was not rebuffing the central bank.
He said he had merely pointed out "to avoid confusion among the populace and certainly not to 'reply' (to the bank)" that the government had the final say.
"The government is in complete agreement with the central bank on the necessity of approving the mini-budget," he said.

Prodi's centre-left government passed a tough 62.5 trillion lira ($37 billion) 1997 budget at the end of last year as part of a campaign to qualify as a founding member of EMU, planned for launch in 1999.
But it is widely accepted that the budget did not do enough to put Italy's finances in order.

In its report, the central bank said: "In the absence of further measures, the reduction of the ratio, compared to the 1996 level, may not surpass three percentage points." ((-- Rome newsroom 396 678 2501))
